name: The Original Position
statement: To find just principles, imagine choosing them without knowing who in society you will turn out to be.
statementAccent: without knowing who in society you will turn out to be
meaning: The original position is a central device in the political philosophy of John Rawls, introduced in his 1971 book A Theory of Justice as part of his theory of justice as fairness. It is a hypothetical thought experiment in which rational, free, and equal parties come together to choose the fundamental principles of justice that will govern their society, doing so through a fair procedure designed to guarantee impartiality. The distinctive feature of the original position is that the parties choose from behind what Rawls called a veil of ignorance: they are deprived of all knowledge of their own particular circumstances, including their social class, natural talents, race, sex, generation, and even their conception of the good life. Because no one knows who they will turn out to be, no one can tailor the principles to their own advantage, and the choice is forced to be fair to all. The original position is Rawls's reworking of the social contract tradition's state of nature, a modern device for modeling a fair agreement on principles of justice. Rawls argued that parties in this position, reasoning cautiously, would choose his two principles of justice, including equal basic liberties and the difference principle. The original position became one of the most influential and discussed ideas in modern political philosophy.
mechanism: The original position works by constructing a choice situation whose conditions guarantee that the principles selected are fair. Rawls imagines representatives of the members of a society coming together to agree on the basic principles that will structure their common life. To ensure the agreement is impartial rather than a bargain skewed by existing advantages, he places the parties behind a veil of ignorance that hides from them everything about their own particular identity and situation: they do not know their wealth or social position, their natural abilities or disabilities, their gender or race, which generation they belong to, or even their own values and conception of the good. They know general facts about human society, economics, and psychology, but nothing that would let them choose principles to favor their own case. Under these conditions, since any party might turn out to occupy any position in society, including the worst-off, Rawls argues they would reason by a form of maximin, seeking to make the worst possible outcome as good as it can be, and would therefore choose principles guaranteeing equal basic liberties for all and permitting inequalities only when they benefit the least advantaged, the difference principle. The fairness of the outcome derives from the fairness of the procedure, which is why Rawls calls his theory justice as fairness. The veil of ignorance is thus the engine that turns self-interested choice into impartial justice.

examples.text: Parties choose principles of justice without knowing their own class, talents, race, sex, or conception of the good.
Because no one can tailor principles to their own case, the impartial procedure yields principles fair to all.
Since any party might be the worst-off, Rawls argues they reason by maximin and choose principles protecting the least advantaged.

variants.name: The two principles
variants.text: The equal basic liberties and the difference principle that Rawls argues would be chosen in the original position.

variants.name: Harsanyi's utilitarian challenge
variants.text: John Harsanyi's argument that parties would maximize average utility rather than reason by maximin.

whyItMatters: The original position is one of the most influential devices in twentieth-century political philosophy, a powerful and intuitive method for reasoning about justice, fairness, and impartiality. By asking what principles people would choose if they did not know their own place in society, Rawls gave a vivid procedure for stripping away the biases of self-interest and privilege and modeling what a genuinely fair agreement on the basic terms of social life would look like. This reworking of the social contract tradition revived normative political philosophy, offered a compelling alternative to utilitarianism, and provided the framework from which Rawls derived his two principles of justice, including the difference principle. The original position and its veil of ignorance have entered wider moral and political reasoning as a general test of fairness, invoked far beyond Rawls's specific theory whenever people ask what rules one would accept without knowing where one would stand under them. It has also generated a vast critical literature that has shaped the field. As the thought experiment that models impartial choice of the principles of justice, the original position is a cornerstone of contemporary political philosophy.

working.text: imagine free and equal representatives coming together to choose the basic principles of justice for their society.
deprive them of all knowledge of their own class, talents, race, sex, and conception of the good.
have them reason, unable to favor their own case, to principles fair to all, such as Rawls's two principles.

limits: The original position is powerful but heavily contested. A central objection concerns the maximin reasoning Rawls attributes to the parties: John Harsanyi argued that rational choosers behind the veil, treating each possible identity as equally likely, would maximize average utility rather than protect the worst-off, and so would not choose Rawls's principles, so whether the original position really yields the difference principle is disputed. The communitarian philosopher Michael Sandel argued that the parties, stripped of their attachments, values, and identities, presuppose an incoherent unencumbered self, abstracted from the very things that constitute a moral agent. Others note that because the parties are so denuded of individuality that they are essentially identical, the supposed choice is really just Rawls's own reasoning rather than a genuine agreement. The device is a hypothetical thought experiment, not a historical event or an actual bargain. So the original position robustly models impartial choice of principles of justice, understood as a contested device whose reasoning, conception of the person, and conclusions are all debated.
misreadings: The original position is not a historical event or an actual meeting; it is a hypothetical thought experiment for modeling fair choice. It does not indisputably yield Rawls's principles, since Harsanyi argued the parties would instead maximize average utility. And the veil-stripped parties are not an obviously coherent picture of a person, as Sandel's unencumbered-self critique charges, so treating the original position as a real bargain, as certainly producing the difference principle, or as resting on an unproblematic view of the self, misreads a contested device for reasoning about justice.
origin: A hypothetical thought experiment introduced by John Rawls in his 1971 book A Theory of Justice, in which parties choose principles of justice behind a veil of ignorance; a reworking of the social contract for modeling fairness.
